title: Why the job got heavier
paras: So — why did the job get heavier? Feeling buried is almost universal, and rarely a sign you're bad at the job. More often you're the conscientious one, trusted with the difficult files, and the work has outgrown the way the day is organised. Managing workload is a set of learnable habits, the sooner the better — it's what's kept me and colleagues on top of the work for four decades.

And planning really has got more demanding, so don't treat the pressure as a personal failing. One modest application now draws a far longer list of consultees than a generation ago — ecology, drainage, heritage, highways, flood risk, nutrient neutrality, biodiversity net gain, viability — each with its own report, consultant and timetable. Policy has thickened nationally and locally and shifts constantly, so staying current is work in itself. Committees and the public scrutinise more, and it all has to be answered in writing, on the record. Speed expectations have jumped — a week has become the same afternoon — and teams do it with fewer planners than ten years ago, so the load per head has climbed.

None of that is your fault — but that's a starting point, not an excuse. A better planner wouldn't find it easy; they'd just have a system. Mine I learned the hard way: early on I let the phone and inbox set my day and went home busy for nine hours with almost nothing finished. The fix was small — each morning I picked, on paper, the one report or letter to finish that day, and gave it an hour before opening my email. Work that used to slip for weeks got done, and the emails waited happily until nine.

title: The interrupted day
paras: Now, the interrupted day. The enemy isn't volume, it's fragmentation. Everything feels urgent at once and throws up interruptions — the agent ringing about the barn mid committee report, the email pulling you off an appeal statement, the colleague whose quick question isn't. Each feels small, but the real cost is the ten minutes afterwards finding your place again in an argument you'd half-built in your head. Do that a dozen times and a day that should have made one finished report gives you three half-finished ones.

The planners who cope don't answer every interruption instantly, because most don't deserve it. The barn will keep an hour; tomorrow's committee report needs an unbroken run. Holding that line politely — "I'm on a deadline, can I call you back at two" — is a genuinely useful skill, and it sits happily with being helpful. Being available to everyone all the time just lets the loudest voice set your priorities, and that's rarely the most important thing on your desk.

title: Deciding what matters first
paras: So how do you decide what matters first? The instinct is to grab whatever shouted last, or whatever's quickest — both dangerous. Better to sort the day by two questions: what has a genuine external deadline, and what carries the most consequence if it goes wrong? Planning hands you plenty of hard fixed points — determination dates, committee cycles, appeal timetables, consultation periods — and those are the skeleton. A statement due at the Inspectorate on Thursday isn't negotiable; a committee report three weeks out can wait a few days.

Beyond the fixed dates, separate the important from the merely urgent. A same-day email is urgent but often trivial; a difficult judgement on a contentious application isn't urgent today, yet it'll shape a scheme worth more than a hundred emails — so give it protected time before it becomes a panic. What works: each morning, before the inbox, write down the two or three things that must genuinely move, and treat the rest as optional until they're done. A short, honest list beats an elaborate system you never keep up.

title: The inbox, and other people’s expectations
paras: The inbox, and other people's expectations. For most planners, email is where the day is quietly lost. Watched as a live feed, every message interrupts you; treat it instead as a task done in blocks, two or three times a day at times you choose. Turn off the pop-up notification, and handle each message once — answer it, file it, or note it on your list — rather than reading it, worrying, and reading it again later.

Underneath that is expectations, where planners make a rod for their own backs: reply within the hour and you teach everyone the hour is the standard. So set one you can sustain, early and pleasantly. Tell a new client you pick up messages at set points, that a considered answer takes time, and that you'll always say when a substantive reply is coming. A short holding line — "received, I'll come back to you properly by Thursday" — buys the time to do it well, and reassures more than a hasty half-answer. Managing expectations isn't evasion; it's the difference between an adviser and a switchboard.

title: Good enough, and the perfectionism trap
paras: Good enough, and the perfectionism trap. Planners are conscientious, and that has a shadow side: time vanishes polishing work past the point where it changes anything. Making every document perfect sounds admirable, but done indiscriminately it's ruinous — the effort you pour into gilding a routine report is stolen from the appeal that genuinely needs it. The skill isn't lowering your standards; it's matching the effort to what the task warrants.

Some work has to be right to the last comma, because an inspector reads it, an inquiry tests it, or it's relied on legally — an appeal statement, a committee report on a finely balanced major, a section 106 head of terms. But much daily work doesn't: an uncontentious householder report needs to be clear, correct and proportionate, not a masterpiece the client isn't paying for. The junior gives everything maximum effort and burns out; the seasoned hand gives the right effort to the right things and lasts. That's not corner-cutting — it's judgement, which is what we're paid for.

title: Getting work off your own plate
paras: Getting work off your own plate. If you manage or work with others, a lot of trouble comes from doing things yourself that someone else could — because explaining feels slower, or you doubt they'll do it right. Both are false economies: the hour you save today, you repay many times over across a year of routine work a junior could have done, and learned from. Delegation isn't offloading; it develops people, and a team that shares the load beats one indispensable planner heading for exhaustion.

The trick is to hand over a whole defined task, with a clear brief and real responsibility — not half of it under supervision that costs you as much attention as doing it yourself. Give the assistant the site visit and first draft, tell them what good looks like, and let them make correctable mistakes while the stakes are low, resisting the urge to rewrite it all in your own voice. The same goes for specialists even as a sole practitioner: brief the ecologist or highways consultant and let them own their piece, rather than holding every discipline in your head. Knowing what only you can do, and letting go of the rest, isn't a loss of control — it's what control looks like.

title: Protecting the thinking time
paras: Protecting the thinking time. Your most valuable work — weighing a balanced case, structuring an appeal, working through a knotty policy conflict — needs uninterrupted concentration, which is exactly what a busy office destroys. Leave it to the gaps that survive the interruptions and you'll do it badly, late at night, tired. Treat concentrated work as an appointment with yourself: block a period when you're sharpest, protect it as fiercely as a meeting with an important client, and spend it on the one thing that most needs your best attention.

How you protect it matters less than that you do — the first ninety minutes before the phones start, a day a week from home, a booked meeting room, or telling colleagues you're not to be disturbed between ten and half past eleven unless something's on fire. Turn off the email, put the phone out of reach, and give the hard task the run it needs. You'll do more in that protected hour than in three fragmented ones, and the difference in quality is what clients and inspectors notice, even when they couldn't say why.

title: Habits that last a career
paras: This comes down to habits that last, because planning is a marathon, not a sprint. The planner who works until eight, answers emails at midnight and never switches off isn't more committed than the one who works hard and then stops — just nearer the point where the quality of the work, and the judgement, slips without them noticing. Take the warning signs seriously the moment they show: small mistakes in careful work, dreading the inbox, comfortable deadlines suddenly feeling tight, a shortening temper, always feeling behind. None means you're failing; each says adjust the system before the load does real damage.

And the fix is rarely heroic effort — usually the opposite: take the protected time more seriously, be firmer about what's genuinely urgent, hand off more routine work, and be honest with clients and managers about what's realistic and when. A sustainable pace isn't the enemy of good work; over anything longer than a fortnight, it's the precondition for it. The planners still sharp and still trusted with the difficult files after thirty or forty years are almost never those who worked the longest hours — they learned, early and the hard way, to stay in control of the work rather than let it control them. It's a skill, and worth learning sooner.

title: Key lessons
paras: To finish, the key lessons in one place.

One: the pressure is real, not a personal failing — planning's grown heavier with fewer staff, so meet it with a system, not guilt. Two: fight fragmentation, not just volume; you don't owe every interruption an instant answer. Three: build the day around fixed points and consequence — determination dates, committee cycles, appeal timetables — and give important work protected time before it turns urgent. Four: write the short list first, and do the most important thing before opening email. Five: treat email as a task, not a feed — blocks, notifications off, each message handled once. Six: set expectations you can sustain, and let a holding reply beat a hasty half-answer.

Seven: match effort to task — an appeal statement earns the last comma, a routine householder report just needs to be proportionate. Eight: delegate whole tasks and let people learn. Nine: guard your thinking time — deep work needs an uninterrupted block. Ten: watch the warning signs and adjust the system rather than run harder. And eleven: pace it for forty years — a sustainable pace is the precondition for good work over a career, and the planners still sharp at the end are rarely those who worked the longest hours.
